'''''Plumbago auriculata''''', the '''Cape leadwort''',<ref name = RHSPF/> '''blue plumbago''' or '''Cape plumbago''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] Plumbaginaceae, [[native plant|native]] to South Africa and Mozambique.<ref name="Botanica 691">"Botanica. The Illustrated AZ of over 10000 garden plants and how to cultivate them", p  691. Könemann, 2004. {{ISBN|3-8331-1253-0}}</ref><ref name="Vermeulen 216">Nico Vermeulen:"The Complete Encyclopedia of Container Plants", p. 216. Rebo International, Netherlands, 1998. {{ISBN|90-366-1584-4}}</ref>

The [[Botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]] ''auriculata'' means "with ears", referring to the shape of the leaves.,<ref name=RHSLG>{{cite book|last=Harrison|first=Lorraine|title=RHS Latin for gardeners|year=2012|publisher=Mitchell Beazley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=9781845337315|pages=224}}</ref> leaf venation - reticulate.

==Description==
''Plumbago auriculata'' is an [[evergreen]] [[shrub]], often grown as a [[vine|climber]], ascending rapidly to {{convert|6|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} tall by {{convert|3|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} wide in nature, though much smaller when cultivated as a [[houseplant]].<ref name=RHSAZ>{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1405332965|pages=1136}}</ref>  The leaves are a glossy green and grow to {{convert|5|cm|0|abbr=on}} long.<ref name="Botanica 691"/><ref name="Vermeulen 216"/> The stems are long, thin, and climbing. The leaves alternate and are 2–5 cm.

===Inflorescences=== 
The [[petal|corolla]] with five petal-like lobes is about 2 cm wide and can be pale blue, blue or violet in color. There also variations with white (''P. auriculata'' var. ''alba'') or deep blue (''P. auriculata'' 'Royal Cape') flowers. The flowers are complete and [[Plant reproductive morphology|bisexual]], and are arranged in [[corymb]]-like [[raceme]]s.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://plantdatabase.kpu.ca/plant/plantDetail/1365|title=Plant Database}}</ref>

The [[sepal]]s and petals are connate while the [[pistil]] is [[adnation|adnate]]. The [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]] of the flower is superior and the flower has regular symmetry. It has basal placentation, with 1 locule and 5 carpels. It flowers mostly in the summer, but in the right conditions it can bloom year-round.<ref>[https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/plumbago-auriculata/ Plumbago auriculata] by The North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox</ref>

==Distribution==
Native to South Africa, it extends from the [[Southern Cape]] region to [[Eastern Cape]] and [[KwaZulu-Natal]]. It can also be found in [[Gauteng]] and the adjoining areas of [[Free State (province)|Free State]] and the [[North West Province]]. There is also an isolated occurrence in [[Mpumalanga]]. Typically the species grows in bushes or thickets. As an ornamental plant, it is widespread today in the tropics and subtropics (including the Mediterranean region).<ref>Andreas Bärtels: Color Atlas of Tropical Plants . Ulmer, Stuttgart 1989, ISBN 3-8001-3448-9 .</ref>

==Biology==
It is visited by various [[butterfly|butterflies]]. Their leaves serve as food for the caterpillar of the [[hummingbird hawk-moth]]. Conversely, the sticky sepals sometimes catch animals up to the size of a housefly. It is believed that the ''Plumbago'' species living today are very similar to the first ancestors of ''[[Drosera]]'' and other [[carnivorous plant]]s.<ref>Jan Schlauer: "New" data relating to the evolution and phylogeny of some carnivorous plant families . In: Carnivorous Plant Newsletter . tape 26, 1997, ISSN  0190-9215, p. 34-38 .</ref>

==Phytochemistry==
Many secondary metabolites have been discovered and isolated from ''Plumbago auriculata'' such as [[plumbagin]] and palmitic acids.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=de Paiva|first1=Selma Ribeiro|last2=Figueiredo|first2=Maria Raquel|last3=Kaplan|first3=Maria Auxiliadora Coelho|date=2005-07-01|title=Isolation of secondary metabolites from roots of Plumbago auriculata Lam. by countercurrent chromatography|journal=Phytochemical Analysis|language=en|volume=16|issue=4|pages=278–281|doi=10.1002/pca.841|pmid=16042155|bibcode=2005PChAn..16..278D |issn=1099-1565}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
In [[temperateness|temperate]] regions, it may be grown outside in frost free areas, otherwise under glass. It grows best in full sun to part shade.

The species<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Plumbago auriculata''|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/13333/Plumbago-auriculata/Details | accessdate=23 February 2020}}</ref> and the white-flowered form ''P. auriculata'' [[form (botany)|f.]] ''alba''<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Plumbago auriculata'' f. ''alba''|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/258158/Plumbago-auriculata-f-alba/Details | accessdate=23 February 2020}}</ref> have both gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 80 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | accessdate = 7 May 2018}}</ref>

''Plumbago auriculata'' can be propagated sexually by seeds and asexually by cutting in summer. It needs well-aerated soil and light and prefers acidic soil.
